OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain and Shri Syed Abdul Malik, 
former Members of this House. 
Shrimati Bedavati passed away on 16th December, 2000, at the age of 79. 
Bom in North Lakhimpur, Assam, November, 1911, Shrimati Buragohain had 
her education at Dibrugarh and Bethune College, Calcutta, She was 
Headmistress, Government Girls M.C. School, Jorhat and was President of 
Tara Rama Dhyani L.P. School in 1952-53. She was a Member of the 
Central Social Welfare Board from 1954 to 1959. She was also associated 
with various social welfare organisations. Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain 
represented the State of Assam in this House from April, 1954 to April, 1960 
and again from April, 1960 to April, 1966. In the passing away of Shrimati 
Bedavati Buragohain, the country has lost a noted teacher and social worker. 
Shri Syed Abdul Malik passed away on  20th December, 2000, at the age 
of 81. Born at Naharani Village, Sibsagar, Assam January 1919. Shri Malik 
had his education at Cotton College, Guwahati. A teacher by profession, Shri 
Malik founded the Kuralguri High School in 1950 and served as its 
Headmaster during 1950-51. He was Professor of Assamese language and 
literature from 1951 to 1976 and also served as Head of the Department of 
Assamese, J.B. College, Jorhat. He was also a noted director actor and writer 
of screenplays for the cinema. Shri Malik had also several publications to his 
credit and represented India at the Asian Writers Conference in 1956-57. 
Shri Malik was also Editor of Assamese Encyclopedia, and literary magazines 
Taigam' and 'Zam Zam'. He received several cultural and literary awards, 
including the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1972. He was conferred the 
Padmashree in 1984 and Padmabhushan in 1992. Shri Syed Abdul Malik 
represented the State of Assam in this House from April, 1976 to April, 1982. 
In the passing away of Shri Syed 
1 

RAJYA SABHA (21 December, 2000] 
Abdul Malik, the country has lost a noted litterateur, an eminent linguist and 
a dedicated social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain and 
Shri Syed Abdul Malik. I request the Members to rise in their places and 
observe silence as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute} 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the

ORAL ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Annual Plan allocation to Orissa 
*461. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Annual Plan  of many states including Orissa 
State has been drastically reduced; 
(b) whether it is because the State due to its financial constraints could not 
mobilise the resources; and 
(c) if so, whether Government are planning for any remedial measures to 
support to this category of financial weak States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DE PARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE 
REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF 
PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
2 

[21 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. States* (including Orissa) Plan outlays for the current year 2000-01 
have been finalized in consultation with the States concerned taking into 
consideration (i) the trend of aggregate actual resource mobilisation for the Plan 
of the State over the firs t three years of the Ninth Plan; and (ii) a realistic 
estimate of resources available for financing the Plan. Since most of the States 
had already budgeted relatively higher Plan size prior to holding of Annual Plan 
discussions, the more realistic Plan size based on identifiable resources that 
was finally agreed upon in accordance with the criteria indicated above has been 
termed the "Core Plan". During State Plan discussions that States were 
encouraged to mobilize additional resources to achieve a Plan size higher than 
the Core Plan size. At the same time, Core Plan outlays for 2000*01 are 
higher than previous year's revised approved Plan outlays in respect of all the 
States except Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur and Punjab. A statement 
giving State-wise details of revised approved outlay for 1999-2000 and approved 
core Plan outlay for 2000-01 is at statement-I (See below). 
(b) The Mid Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan revealed that as 
compared to the originally approved ou tlays, there were shortfalls in the 
resources mobilized by the States (including Orissa) during the first three years of 
the Ninth Five Year Plan. This was mainly because there had been a deterioration 
in the contribution of their own funds of the States to finance Plans, leading to 
increased dependence on borrowings to finance their Plan. The shortfall in the 
contribution of own funds of the States had in turn been mainly due to a 
deterioration in States' Balance from Current Revenue (BCR) and 
unsatisfactory performance of State Level Enterprises. A statement indicating 
the shares of central assistance, State's own funds and borrowings in the 
financing of the State Plan Outlay for Orissa is attached as statement-II (See 
below). 
(c) Planning Commission have been impressing upon the States to generate 
higher level of own resources inter-alia by improving the performance of State Level 
Enterprises, increasing tax and non-tax revenue and also by curtailing their non-
plan expenditure so that 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2000] 
sufficient funds are available to finance the plan. In addition, joint efforts by the 
Centre and the states were initiated during 1999-2000 to evolve a strategy to 
address the fiscal issues confronting the financially weaker States in the 
form of a package of financial assistance to be provided by the centre alongwith 
an appropriate time bound programme of medium term fiscal reforms to be 
undertaken by the States. Thirteen States including Orissa have so far entered 
into an agreement (Memorandum of Understanding) with the Centre with a view to 
implement the fiscal reforms aiming at progressively improving the finances of 
the States. List of States which have entered into MoUs for fiscal reform is 
attached as statement-Ill. (See below). The Centre has made available financial 
assistance of Rs. 4490 crores so far to help these States tide over short-term 
difficulties and undertake fiscal reforms. Out of this, Rs. 300 crores has been 
released to Orissa.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The wholesale prices of certain agricultural commodities at some 
selected centres are ruling below the Minimum Support Price (MSP) announced 
by the Government. The fall in prices may be attributed to increased 
availability of certain agricultural commodities in our country and the declining 
trend in international prices of certain agricultural commodities. The cost of 
production has generally been rising because of the increase in wages of labour and 
increase in the prices of inputs such as diesel, fertilizers etc. 
(c) The Government announces MSPs for major agricultural commodities each 
season and organizes purchase operations through public and cooperative agencies 
viz. Food Corporation of India (FO) for paddy, wheat and coarse cereals. Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI) for cotton, Jute Corporation of India (JCI) for jute, 
NAFED for oilseeds and pulses and Tobacco Board for tabacco. Those 
commodities, which are perishable in nature and which are grown mainly locally 
or where the cost differentia! varies substantially from State to State are covered 
under Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) of the Government. Large quantities 
of cereals etc. have been procured under the MSP scheme and procurement of 
certain commodities is continuing. 
With a view to protect the interests of the fanners from cheap imports into 
the country, the tariff levels have been bound for primary agricultural products 
and edible oils, with a few exceptions at 100 per cent, ISO per cent and 300 per 
cent respectively. The Government has been using instruments of trade to 
discourage the imports and encourage exports wherever necessary, and protect the 
interests of the farmers.

†*464. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': WiU the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage share of Government agencies in marketing of 
agricultural products; 
(b) whether there is a need to increase this share; 
(c) if so, how much and by when; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (d) The Food 
Corporation of India and State Governments/its Agencies mainly procure 
wheat and rice under price support operations. During the last few years, 
around 12 percent to 20 percent of the entire production of wheat and rice has 
been procured by them. Besides, the National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing 
Federation of India Limited (NAFED), which is the apex institution of 
marketing cooperatives in the country, is also engaged in marketing of 
agricultural commodities by implementing the Price Support Scheme for 
oilseeds, including copra, and pulses and the Market Intervention Scheme for 
horticultural and agricultural commodities which are perishable in nature. 
The extent of procurement and sales of agricultural produce by 
Government/its Agencies would depend upon the price situation prevailing in 
the country. Therefore, it is not feasible to indicate any percentage share for the 
Government agencies in respect of .procurement and sales of agricultural 
produce and products. In view of this, not time limit in this regard can be 
indicated.

Bharatiya Cattle Breeds 
3463. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that America, Brazil, Mexico maintain herds of 
Brahman, Krishna, Cows/Bulls which are imported there from India; 
(b) whether the American Brahman breeders Association in Taxas encourages 
pure breeds of Bharatiya Cows/Bulls; 
(c) whether our native breeds are becoming extinct and/or used for exotic 
breeding with foreign blood, thereby loosing their characteristics of Drought 
Power; and 
(d) whether cross breed male calves are not found usable in 
agriculture or transportation and reach slaughter houses in young 
age? 
THE    MINISTER    OF    STATE    IN    THE    MINISTRY    OF 
AGRICULTURE   (DR.   DEBENDRA   PRADHAN);   (a)   and   (b) Yes, 
Sir. 
(c) and (d) Extinction of breeds because of rapid changes in the socio-economic 
and agroclimatic conditions across the world is a global phenomenon. Since it 
is not possible to meet the rising demand for milk of the fast growing human 
population in the country by exclusively following selective breeding of 
indigenous cattle breeds, it is necessary to infuse exotic germ-plasm in a part of the 
low producing non-descript indigenous cattle through crossbreeding. The 
population of indigenous cattle for outnumber the crossbred stock and the 
policy of the Government has been to insist on having a balanced 
improvement of cattle, both for milk and draught. Crossbred males are suitable 
for agriculture and transportation where the work-surface is not too muddy and 
when they are put to work during cooler hours of the day. Legislation exists in 
most of the states prohibiting slaughter of male calves at an early age.

21 November, 2000 at the invitation of H.E. Shri Krishan Kant, Vice

Brig. Gen. Pyi Sone, Minister for Commerce and H.E. U Khin Maung Kyaw, 
Dy. Minister of Industry-II, and other senior officials.

bilateral, regional and international issues. They discussed measures to create 
favourable conditions for the rapid development of bilateral relations. 
3. Relations between India and Myanmar are civilizational in nature and 
rooted in a common cultural and religious heritage and geographical 
contiguity. Leaders of both countries have always maintained a tradition of 
high level exchanges and personal rapport. With the visit by General Maung 
Aye this process has been enhanced. 
4. In Delhi, H.E. General Maung Aye and Daw Mya Mya San were 
accorded a warm ceremonial welcome by H.E. Shri Krishan Kant, Vice 
President of India and Shrimati Suman Krishan Kant. H.E, General Maung

Vice President, H.E. Shri Atal Bihari  Vajpayee, Prime Mi nister, H.E. Shri 
Jaswant Singh, Minister of External Affairs, H.E. Shri L.K. Advani, Home 
Minister, Shri Omar Farooq Abdulla, Minister of State for Commerce & 
Industry, and Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, Leader of Opposition. 
5. The discussions between the Prime Minister and the Vice Chairman, 
State Peace & Development Council covered a wide range of areas, including 
economic cooperation, trade, cro ss border projects and activities, 
international, terrorism, drug trafficking, cooperation in the field of culture, 
human resource development, science and technology, and regional 
cooperation within the framework of BIMST-EC, of which both countries 
are members, as also under the

relations. Both sides reaffirmed their desire to promote bilateral relations to a 
qualitatively higher and dynamic stage. They also agreed that they could 
benefit from various regional cooperation programmes in which they are 
participating, such as BIMST-EC and India-ASEAN cooperation. 
6. -The two sides agreed to take st eps to ensure peace" and tranquillity 
along the India-Myanmar border, and to give content to cross border 
cooperation, which would directly benefit populations living on both sides of 
the border. They recognized the need to establish the necessary infrastructure 
in terms of cross border transport and communication links, promote more 
frequent exchanges both at the government and people-to-people level, and 
actively encourage the business communities of both countries to take 
advantage of the many economic complementarities between the two 
countries. The Tamu-Kalemyo highway which will link India's northeast with 
the western part of the Myanmar and beyond would contribute singnificantly 
to this cross border cooper ation. The highway is expected to be handed over

(b) and (c) Making the administration corruption free, accountable, 
transparent and more effective has been on the agenda of the Government 
which is fully committed to provide clean administration and to eradicate 
corruption at all levels. In the Ministries/Departments etc of the Central 
Government, the Secretary and the Head of the Department concerned is 
responsible for ensuring probity and integrity in their respective organisations. 
A three pronged strategy of Surveillance, Prevention and Punitive/ Deterrent 
action is followed by the Government in this regard. Recognising that an 
important aspect of Preventive Vigilance is to ensure transparency in public 
administration, measures of administrative reforms such as introduction of 
Citizens' Charters and setting up of Facilitation Centres have been initiated. The 
review and simplification of laws, rules and procedures has also been taken 
up. The punitive actions being taken under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 
1988 duly supported by various rules governing the service conditions of 
public servants, also act as a deterrent  against corruption. An anti-corruption 
unit is functioning in the Prime Mini ster's Office since 1997 to monitor 
complaints of corruption received in that Office. 
2. During the mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan, Planning 
Commission has also recognized that one of the main factors which hinder plan 
implementation is governance which, infer^alia, include corruption. Planning 
Commission has, therefore, taken Sn initiative to indicate that factors which tend 
to retard economic development, and to determine the conditions that should 
be established for successful execution of the Plan and further private

situation and Constitued a Group to study and suggest procedural reforms in

3. Some of the other major initiatives taken by the Government in the 
recent past towards eradication of  corruption from public services, inter-alia 
include introduction of Central Vigilance Commission Bill on 20.12.1999 in 
the Lok Sabha. Apart from this, the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000 has 
also been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 25.7.2000 to bring greater 
transparency and accountability in the functioning of the Government. 
Further, the Lokpal Bill, 1998 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 3rd 
August, 1998 and lapsed on the dissolution of the House on 26.4.1999. The 
Government has already initiated steps for the enactment of suitable 
legislation relating to Lokpal. 
4. However, the drive against corruption in public services is a continuing 
process. The policies formulated in this regard are modified from time to 
time in order to make them more effective and responsive to the changing 
environment.

PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN

GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOUFTE): The Economic 
Reforms process initiated in the country in 1990s also witnessed a move to 
decentralize governance to the local level. Seventy Third and 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2000] 
Seventy Fourth Constitutional Amendment Acts bestowed Cons titutional 
status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). Panchayati Raj Bodies which 
came into existence in the States pursuant to the Constitutional Amendments 
were delegated administrative and finanical powers in areas which are critical to 
the livelihoods of the population. The PRIs have also been given a greater say 
in execution and monitoring of developmental process. 
Major poverty alleviation programmes have been restructured to address the 
needs of the people in a more focused manner. Areas Development Programmes 
have been given a fillip. Basic services to the people have been sought to be 
provided under the Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). rural 
connectivity which enables people not only to increase their incomes but also 
diversify the livelihood options has been given a high priority under the PMGY. 
Social security provided through the National Social Assistance Programme 
(NSAP) has been widened and deepened. These changes are expected to enable 
the community at large to take advantage of the reform process and better their 
living conditions in the rural areas. 
Economic reform is a continuous process involving changes in a wide range 
of policies and procedures. The board direction of reforms has been outlined in 
the Ninth Five Year Plan and the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan 
documents. Further direction would be provided in the Tenth Five Year Plan, on 
which work has just commenced. Detailed reforms regarding each sector are being 
announced as and when required.

Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation is the nodal agency for 
monitoring the implementation of Central Sector Projects costing Rs. 20 crores and 
above. Proposals for these projects are, however, formulated by the Public Sector 
Enterprise^Ministries of the Government of India. While the techno-economic 
feasibility reports relating to the project proposals are appraised by the Planning 
Commission (Project Appraisal and Management Division) from the angles of 
demand and supply of products and services, availability of resources etc., such 
proposals are also examined simultaneously by the Ministry of Finance (Plan 
Finance Division), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (Project 
Monitoring Division), Ministry of Environment and Forests, etc. before these 
are considered in the Public Investment Board for further submission to the 
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. The time frames of the projects and the 
need to complete them within these time frame and costs are kept in view along 
with other relevant aspects while considering and clearing them. 
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation monitors the 
implementation of the Central Sector Projects with a view to identifying the 
bottlenecks in their implementation and apprising the authorities concerned of 
them for remedial action. The Ministry brings out monthly Flash Reports, 
Exception Reports and detailed Status Reports on the implementation of these 
projects. These reports, among other things, highlight those projects which 
have

attention of all concerned for their completion without any further delay and cost

total number of projects on the monitor of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation is 463 as on 1/10/2000. The enclosed Statement given the 
distribution of projects in various sectors under implementation (See below). The 
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation have identified the 
following measures to ensure that projects are completed on schedule and within 
the Costs approved:

administrative Ministries and follow up with the State Governments (for 
acquisition of land and provision of infrastructure facilities like water and 
power, ensuring law & order at project sites, etc.)* consultants and other 
concerned agencies to minimise delays; 
(iii) setting up of an Empowered Committee in each administrative Ministry 
for resolution of problems;

DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA (West Bengal): Sir, I have no basic 
objection to these two Bills which have been proposed. But I am taking 
advantage of the discussion to rais e certain issues, to which I hope, 
our hon. Finance Minister would re spond. My first question is this. 
Now, we nave had the so-called refo rms for more than ten years. In 
the earty days of the reforms, when ever I asked the Finance Minister 
about something critically, he used to say, "Wait for some more time. 
Give us some more time. Initially it is going to be painful. Then it will be 
all right." For almost ten years, they have been taking the same ptea. 
What we are expecting the Finance Minister to do Is to make a 
comparison between the two types of statistics; one with the figures of 
the 80s and the other with the figures of the 90s, with 1900-91 as the 
base year. And, if we look at the figures which emerge from that, you 
will see that, on most counts, we have done worse 
324 

[21 December, 2000]    RAJYA SABHA 
in the 90s than in the 80s. For exampl e, if we take the industry growth 
rate, it is much less than what it was in the 80s. Again, the agriculture 
growth rate is less; the savings rate is less; the investment rate Is less. 
Now, these are the major macro economic indicators for any economy. 
All these macro economic indicato rs have failed in the 90s in 
comparison to the 80s. On GDP, I agree that it shows six or seven per 
cent higher than what it was in the 80s; it may be slightly more or 
slightly less. But the basic question is: If agriculture is not doing very 
well, if industry is not doing very well, then, how can the GDP do well? 
It may be that we have done well in the service sector. Now, the 
service sector can be interpreted in many ways. There are hotels; 
there are computers; there is transport and all that in the service 
sector. In a country hke India, we do not have the service sector tike 
that in the U.S. or in England or other places. So, there has to be a 
realistic assumption of the GDP growth; we have to see whether the 
GDP captures the actual measure,  say, the people's welfare and well-
being. And, how can you do it If the agriculture sector is not doing very 
well? 
Recently, our hon. Prime Minister made a very interesting 
statement. He said that for the next month, the rate of growth estimate 
is tow. He wanted this to be nine per cent. Now, the hon. Prime 
Minister probably does not know much of economics. But those who 
are aware of economics would have to ld the Prime Minister that it is 
not the wish of the Government which can determine the rate of 
growth of a particular economy. A nd if you go by what the hon. Prime 
Minister wishes, then, for achieving a nine per rate of growth, you 
require a 36 per cent rate of savi ng, keeping the capital-output ratio to 
be 4:1, or even keeping it to 3:1, we should have at least 27 per cent 
rate of saving. Only that kind of saving can generate that kind of 
growth. There is a certain relationship between saving and growth. 
And that would be classified into what you want, what could be done 
and all that. But 38 per cent, or even keeping it lower at, say, 27 per 
cent, is also much higher than our present saving rate, which is 22-23 
per cent. This rate is much less than what we require to achieve such 
a rate of growth. So, this Is one question that I am raising. When you 
took through the GDP estimates, how and on what basis are they 
being estimated? And, Is there something wrong with the way in which 
it is being done? I also find It amateurish and casual the way you talk 
about our objectives and all that, not based on real calculation, not 
based on reliable data and other factors. First, we have the provisional 
and quick estimates. Eventually, we have the confirmed estimates.   
The confirmed estimates are

The confirmed estimates should be correct. 
The next point that I am raising is on the question of 
globalisation, I find something funny in this. I am sure, our hon. 
Finance Minister would agree with me , that if you go sector by sector, 
then, everybody is for globalisation for others and not for globalisation 
in their own sector. When we were  discussing the patent issue in 
Parliament, some of our friends in the Government suggested that 
Ayurvedic medicines should be protected from foreign competition. 
Why? if globalisation is good, it should be good for the 
Ayurvedic system also.  The same is  the case with the print media.  
The print media is 
very actively advocating globalisation. But it does not want 
globalisation for itself; and so, the foreign newspapers should be out. i 
am also saying that foreign newspapers should be out; but I am 
consistent. There is a fallacy; there is a double talk in the print media. 
They want globalisation for every body else, but not for themselves. 
Lawyers are the big champions of globalisation all over the country; 
but no foreign lawyer should come. If I believe foreigners are good in 
other sectors, why should I oppose gl obalisation in the sector in which 
I am working? That is the questi on. I am preaching repeatedly that 
globalisation is good for others, but  not for me. This hypocritical 
attitude should be dropped. Whether it is the lawyers or the print media 
or anybody else, we should be consistent in the views that we take on 
globalisation. 
If you take disinvestment, Mr, Finance Minister — I mentioned 
this before - we have had rich experie nce in many countries that have 
gone through disinvestment -- like Chile, Ghana, Mexico, even our 
neighbour, Pakistan and to some extent, Bangladesh. If you put all 
these experiences together - ther e have been many studies; some 
conducted by UNCTAD and some conducted by many other bodies 
and all of them reached the same conclusions -- in all these cases, 
there are stories about price fixation, about squeezing in various 
forms. Whatever we heard now about India with regard to many 
disinvestment programmes, it is t he same experience that we have 
seen in the case of other countries. I would request the Finance 
Minister to look into these experiences in his Ministry and try to see to 
it hat disinvestment is not taken t oo far. I do not understand this drive 
towards disinvestment, frankly speaking. Why should there be 
disinvestment?  Why shouid only the public sector undertakings be
